community-health-worker.intro: Learn to serve communities as a frontline health worker. From home visits to health education to referrals — the role that connects people to the health system and saves lives through prevention.

skillDomains.name: Home Visits
skillDomains.description: The core of the CHW role — meeting people where they live.

skills.name: Conducting a Visit
skills.description: How to enter a home, build trust, and gather useful information.

modules.title: The home visit
modules.content:
The home visit is the primary tool of a Community Health Worker. Done well, it builds trust, catches problems early, and connects families to care.

The structure of a visit

  1. Greet respectfully — ask permission to enter
  2. Explain your purpose
  3. Listen first — what concerns does the family have?
  4. Observe — living conditions, sanitation, food
  5. Check specifically — children's growth, immunisations, pregnancy, chronic illness
  6. Advise — one or two key points, not ten
  7. Refer — if needed, and explain what will happen at the clinic
  8. Record — after you leave, note what you found

modules.title: Building trust in the community
modules.content:
You are a guest

Even when you're the health worker, you're entering someone's home. Respect their space, their time, and their privacy.

Do

  • Greet elders first
  • Speak the local language if you can
  • Accept water if offered
  • Sit when invited
  • Be consistent

Don't

  • Judge their home or choices
  • Give lectures
  • Discuss private information in front of others
  • Make promises you can't keep

steps.q: You arrive at a home and the mother is busy cooking. What do you do?
o: Ask if it's a good time or if you should come back

steps.q: You notice the family has no latrine. What do you do?
o: Listen first and offer practical options

steps.q: A child in the home looks unwell. The mother says it's nothing. What do you do?
o: Ask more questions about symptoms, and refer if there are danger signs
steps.f: Respect the parent, but screen for danger signs.

skillDomains.name: Screening
skillDomains.description: Catch problems early — before they become emergencies.

skills.name: Child Health Screening
skills.description: The signs that mean a child needs urgent care.

modules.title: Danger signs in children
modules.content:
WHO has identified a short list of "general danger signs" that mean a child needs urgent care:

  • Unable to drink or breastfeed
  • Vomiting everything
  • Convulsions (fits)
  • Lethargy or unconsciousness

Any ONE of these means immediate referral.

Other concerning signs

  • Fast breathing
  • Chest indrawing
  • Sunken eyes
  • Skin pinch returning slowly (dehydration)
  • Fever lasting more than 2 days
  • Blood in stool
  • Refusing food for more than a day

steps.q: A 2-year-old is drowsy, difficult to wake, and hasn't eaten since yesterday. What do you do?
o: Immediate referral — this is lethargy, a danger sign
steps.f: Lethargy is a WHO general danger sign. Refer immediately.

steps.q: A child has had diarrhoea for 2 days but is still drinking and playing. What do you do?
o: Advise ORS and continue monitoring at home
steps.f: No danger signs, so home management with ORS and follow-up.

steps.q: A child is having convulsions. What do you do?
o: Protect the child from injury, then refer immediately
steps.f: Protect the child, then refer immediately.

modules.title: Danger signs in pregnancy
modules.content:
These signs mean a pregnant woman needs immediate care:

  • Bleeding from the vagina at any point
  • Severe headache with blurred vision (possible pre-eclampsia)
  • Swelling of face and hands, especially sudden
  • High fever
  • Convulsions
  • Severe abdominal pain
  • Reduced or stopped fetal movement
  • Water breaking before 37 weeks

Encourage all pregnant women to attend antenatal care at least 4 times.

steps.q: A pregnant woman in her third trimester has severe headache and blurred vision. What do you do?
steps.f: Headache with visual changes is a pre-eclampsia red flag.

steps.q: A pregnant woman mentions light bleeding. What do you do?
o: Refer immediately — any bleeding in pregnancy is urgent
steps.f: Any vaginal bleeding in pregnancy needs immediate assessment.

steps.q: A pregnant woman has not attended any antenatal visits at 7 months. What do you do?
o: Understand her barriers and help her access care
steps.f: Understand barriers and help solve them.

skillDomains.name: Health Education
skillDomains.description: Prevention is your most powerful tool.

skills.name: Teaching Methods
skills.description: How to educate adults in a way that sticks.

modules.title: Adults don't learn from lectures
modules.content:
Health education that works uses:

  • Discussion — ask what they already know
  • Demonstration — show, don't just tell
  • Practice — let them try
  • Repetition — same message, multiple visits
  • Local language — always
  • Real examples — from their community

The rule of one

One message per visit. If you try to teach five things, they'll remember none.

modules.title: Core health education topics
modules.content:
Prevention topics you'll teach

  • Handwashing — with soap, at critical times
  • Safe water — boiling, filtering, treating
  • Sanitation — latrine use, disposal of waste
  • Nutrition — exclusive breastfeeding, complementary feeding, balanced diet
  • Immunisation — full schedule for children
  • Malaria prevention — nets, indoor spraying
  • Family planning — methods and access
  • HIV prevention — condoms, testing, treatment

skillDomains.name: Referrals
skillDomains.description: Knowing when and how to refer saves lives.

skills.name: Referral Process
skills.description: How to move a person from the community to the health facility smoothly.

modules.title: The referral chain
modules.content:
CHWs are the bridge between community and clinic.

Steps in a referral

  1. Recognise the need (danger sign, condition beyond your scope)
  2. Explain to the person and family why it's needed
  3. Prepare a referral slip with your findings
  4. Arrange transport if needed
  5. Confirm they actually got there
  6. Follow up after the visit

Referral doesn't end at the door — it ends when the person receives care and returns home.

steps.q: A family refuses to go to the clinic because of the cost. What do you do?
o: Explore options: sliding-scale fees, community fund, referral to free services
steps.f: Address the barrier. There's almost always a solution.

steps.q: You referred a child with danger signs to the clinic yesterday. What do you do today?
o: Follow up — did they go? What was the outcome?
Wait for them to call you

steps.q: A patient is referred but has no transport. What do you do?
steps.f: Transport is a common barrier. Help solve it.

modules.title: Why CHW records matter
modules.content:
Records serve three purposes

  1. Patient care — tracking who needs follow-up
  2. Reporting — showing the health system what's happening at community level
  3. Accountability — proving your work to supervisors and funders

What to record

  • Every visit (date, household, findings)
  • Every referral (date, reason, outcome)
  • Every education session (topic, attendees)
  • Every screening (result, action)

steps.q: You finish a home visit at 4 PM. When do you write the record?
o: Same day, before you forget details
At the end of the week
steps.f: Same day. Memory degrades within hours.

steps.q: A referral didn't result in a visit. What do you record?
o: The referral, and the fact that the family didn't attend, with the reason

steps.q: Your supervisor asks for monthly reports. What should the report contain?
o: All activity: visits, referrals, outcomes, challenges
steps.f: Honest reporting helps the whole system.
